prompt: Where is a Git repository's history kept?
hint: `ls -a` showed it and `ls` did not.

choices.text: In the .git directory inside the project folder
choices.why: Right. Everything Git keeps about this project is in there, and nowhere else.

choices.text: In a hidden file beside each file it tracks
choices.why: There is one directory for the whole project, not a file per file.

choices.text: In ~/.gitconfig, with the name and address
choices.why: That file holds your settings for every repository. No project's history is in it.

choices.text: On GitHub, from the first commit
choices.why: Nothing has been sent anywhere. The repository is local until you choose to share it.

prompt: Somebody deletes the .git directory of a project and leaves every other file alone. What is left?
hint: Which of the three places lives inside .git?

choices.text: Nothing at all; the files go with it
choices.why: The working tree is outside .git and is untouched.

choices.text: The files, with no history behind them
choices.why: Right. The working tree survives; every commit, and the staging area, were inside .git.

choices.text: The history, which Git rebuilds from the files
choices.why: The files are one version. The others existed only in .git.

choices.text: The last commit, since it matches the files on disk
choices.why: Matching is not being stored. The commit objects were in .git.

prompt: Match each place to what it holds.
hint: One description on the right is not one of the three.

pairs.right: The files as you are editing them
The next commit, while it is being put together

right_distractors: The settings that apply to every project

prompt: A colleague says git add means "tell Git to track this file". What does it do that this description misses?
hint: Think about a file that was already tracked.

choices.text: Nothing; tracking is all it does
choices.why: It is also used on files Git has tracked for years, which would make no sense if that were all.

choices.text: It sends the file to the shared server
choices.why: add never touches the network. It copies the file into the staging area on your machine.

choices.text: It saves the file permanently in the history
choices.why: That is what commit does. After add, nothing is in the history yet.

choices.text: It stages this version for the next commit
choices.why: Right. It is used on every change you want committed, new file or not, and it copies the file as it is at that moment.

prompt: git status lists index.html under "Untracked files". What does that mean?
hint: It is on the disk. Is it in any commit?

choices.text: Git sees it, but no commit has it
choices.why: Right. It stays out of every commit until somebody adds it.

choices.text: Git cannot read it
choices.why: Git can read it; it listed it. Nobody has asked Git to keep it.

choices.text: It was deleted since the last commit
choices.why: A deleted file shows as deleted. This one is on the disk and was never committed.

choices.text: It will be included in the next commit automatically
choices.why: Nothing untracked goes into a commit, not even with commit -a.

prompt: The first commit of a repository printed [main (root-commit) 6abda31]. What does root-commit say about it?
hint: Lesson 1 showed what a first commit is missing.

choices.text: It was made by the administrator of the machine
choices.why: Root here has nothing to do with users. Ana made it with her own account.

choices.text: It has no parent: the history starts there
choices.why: Right. Every later commit leads back to this one.

choices.text: It contains every file in the folder, tracked or not
choices.why: It contains what was staged. A commit never includes untracked files.

choices.text: It can no longer be changed, unlike later commits
choices.why: No commit is special in that way. Changing any one changes the ids after it.

prompt: After the first commit, git status says: nothing to commit, working tree ___.
hint: The word for a working tree that matches the last commit.

prompt: Ana types git commit with no -m and closes the editor without writing anything. What happens?
hint: A commit's message is part of the commit.

choices.text: The commit is made with an empty message
choices.why: Git refuses an empty message unless it is told explicitly to allow one.

choices.text: The commit is made with the file names as its message
choices.why: Git invents no message, the same way it invented no author.

choices.text: The staged changes are thrown away
choices.why: They stay staged. Only the commit is cancelled.

choices.text: No commit is made, and the staging area is left as it was
choices.why: Right. Git cancels the commit and nothing is lost.

prompt: index.html is modified and style.css is new. Ana runs git add style.css, then git commit. What is in the commit?
hint: A commit takes the staging area, not the folder.

choices.text: Only style.css
choices.why: Right. The change to index.html stays in the working tree for a commit of its own.

choices.text: Both files, since both changed
choices.why: That is what a system with no staging area would do. Git takes only what was added.

choices.text: Only index.html, since it was already tracked
choices.why: Being tracked does not stage a change. Only add, or commit -a, does.

choices.text: Nothing, because index.html was left unstaged
choices.why: A commit does not need every change staged. It takes what is there.

prompt: git status shows index.html under both "Changes to be committed" and "Changes not staged for commit". How did that happen?
hint: add copies a file at one moment.

choices.text: Git is showing the same change twice
choices.why: They are two different changes: the two git diff commands show different lines.

choices.text: The file was added, then edited again before the commit
choices.why: Right. The staging area holds the version from the moment of add; the later edit is only in the working tree.

choices.text: Two people edited the file at the same time
choices.why: One person can produce this alone, and Ana did.

choices.text: The file was added twice, so it is staged twice
choices.why: A second add replaces the staged copy. It never adds a second one.

prompt: Ana changed "six in the morning" to "half past five", ran git add, then changed it to "half past five, every day" and ran git commit. What does the commit contain?
hint: Which version was in the staging area when commit ran?

choices.text: half past five, every day
choices.why: That version never reached the staging area. It is still only in the working tree.

choices.text: six in the morning
choices.why: That is the last commit's version. The add replaced it in the staging area.

choices.text: half past five
choices.why: Right. The commit took the version add copied, and the later edit is still waiting.

choices.text: Nothing, since the file changed after add
choices.why: Git does not refuse. It commits what is staged and leaves the rest.

prompt: Match each command to the two things it compares.
hint: One pair on the right is compared by neither command.

pairs.right: The working tree against the staging area
The staging area against the last commit

right_distractors: The working tree against the shared server

prompt: index.html is modified and menu.html is new and never added. Ana runs git commit -am "Open every day". What does the commit contain?
hint: -a works on files Git already has.

choices.text: Both files
choices.why: -a skips files that were never tracked, and menu.html never was.

choices.text: Neither, since nothing was staged
choices.why: -a stages the tracked changes itself before committing.

choices.text: Only menu.html, because it is new
choices.why: New is exactly what -a leaves out.

choices.text: Only the change to index.html
choices.why: Right. menu.html stays untracked and still needs its own git add.

prompt: Match each line of git status --short to what it means.
hint: The left column is the staging area; the right column is the working tree.

pairs.right: Untracked: in no commit and not staged

prompt: Ana renames style.css to site.css with a plain mv and commits straight away without adding anything. What does the commit contain?
hint: After the mv, git status showed both changes unstaged.

choices.text: The rename, since Git detects renames
choices.why: Git detects a rename in what was staged. Here nothing was.

choices.text: Neither change, since both were unstaged
choices.why: Right. With nothing staged there is nothing to commit, and Git says so.

choices.text: Only the deletion of style.css
choices.why: The deletion was not staged either. A plain mv stages nothing.

choices.text: A copy of site.css beside the old style.css
choices.why: Nothing was added, so nothing new can appear in the commit.

prompt: The commit summary says rename style.css => site.css (100%). What does the 100% measure?
hint: Git does not record renames. It works them out.

choices.text: How much of the rename has been staged
choices.why: Staging is all or nothing for a file.

choices.text: How similar the new file is to the old one
choices.why: Right. Git compares content, and a file that moved without changing is identical.

choices.text: How sure Git is that git mv was used
choices.why: The same summary appears with add and rm instead of mv. Git cannot tell and does not need to.

choices.text: The share of the project the commit touched
choices.why: That is what the files-changed line counts, not the percentage.

prompt: To delete todo.txt and stage the deletion in one step: git ___ todo.txt
hint: The shell's own word for deleting.

prompt: Put the steps of making one commit of a new file in order.
hint: The history is last.
items: Create the file in the working tree
git status shows it as untracked
git add copies it into the staging area
git commit records what was staged
trap: A file is not in the staging area until add; status only reports.

prompt: Ana fixed a typo in index.html and, in the same file, started a new paragraph that is not ready. She wants a commit with the typo fix only. What does this lesson let her do?
hint: Both changes are in one file, and add copies whole files.

choices.text: Commit with -a, then describe only the fix in the message
choices.why: The commit would contain the unfinished paragraph, whatever the message says.

choices.text: Cut the unfinished lines out, stage, commit, then paste them back
choices.why: Right. add copies the file as it is, so it has to be the version with the fix alone. Lesson 11 shows how to stage part of a file directly.

choices.text: git add index.html, since add only stages finished changes
choices.why: Git has no idea what is finished. add copies the whole file as it is.

choices.text: Nothing; a commit always takes every change in a file
choices.why: The commit takes what is staged, and she controls what the staged file contains.

prompt: Which of these would appear in the next commit if Ana ran git commit now? Choose all that apply.
hint: The first column is the staging area.

choices.text: A  about.html
choices.why: Yes. A in the first column is a new file, staged.

choices.text: M index.html
choices.why: The M is in the second column: modified and not staged.

choices.text: D  todo.txt
choices.why: Yes. A staged deletion goes into the commit.

choices.text: ?? notes.txt
choices.why: Untracked files never go into a commit on their own.

prompt: Which of these commands never changes anything in the repository or the working tree?
hint: It is the one to type whenever you are unsure.

choices.text: git status
choices.why: Right. It only reads and reports.

choices.text: git add
choices.why: add changes the staging area.

choices.text: git rm
choices.why: rm deletes a file and stages the deletion.

choices.text: git restore
choices.why: restore overwrites files in the working tree; lesson 4 is about it.
